item.title: Constitution Bill passes second reading with required 35 votes
item.description: Vijay Narayan , Mansi Chand , Priya Nand , Navitalai Naivalurua , Karishma Kumari , Antornette Vuniuca , Mikaele Liga · 02/10/2026 The Constitution Amendment Bill 2026 has passed its second reading in Parliament after the Government secured the required 35 votes.
item.content:encoded:
Vijay Narayan , Mansi Chand , Priya Nand , Navitalai Naivalurua , Karishma Kumari , Antornette Vuniuca , Mikaele Liga · 02/10/2026

The Constitution Amendment Bill 2026 has passed its second reading in Parliament after the Government secured the required 35 votes.

A total of 38 MPs voted in favour of the Bill, five voted against it, nine abstained and one did not vote.

The Bill will now proceed to its third reading.

A Joint Parliamentary Select Committee led by Prime Minister Rabuka, and Deputy Prime Minister Viliame Gavoka, National Federation Party Leader and MP Professor Biman Prasad, Acting Attorney General Siromi Turaga, Minister for Lands Filimoni Vosarogo, Minister for Information Lynda Tabuya, Minister for Rural and Maritime Development Mosese Bulitavu, Leader of the Opposition Inia Seruiratu and 3 members of the Opposition nominated by the Opposition Leader will have consultations with the people of Fiji over the next 30 days.

The Special Committee will report back to Parliament on 2nd November.

Rabuka says what Parliament discussed today is not just a Bill, but a framework by which people will live, work, raise their families, practise their faith, protect their communities and determine the future of the country.

He says the Constitution must serve the people and respond to the realities they face today and in the future.

Meanwhile, a total of 12 speakers from both the Government and the Opposition spoke on the Bill during the debate.

Opposition Leader, Inia Seruiratu says any new constitutional framework must serve Fiji fairly and democratically for generations and should not be shaped around the interests of the government, opposition or institutions of today.

Seruiratu says constitutional reviews provide an opportunity to change the direction of the country, but there must be a clear understanding of why change is necessary, what needs to change and the implications and benefits of those changes.

He says the process must be guided by good governance, including public participation, consensus, inclusivity, accountability and transparency.

Seruiratu stresses that the Bill is not an ordinary piece of legislation, as it proposes to repeal provisions of the 2013 Constitution, with the exception of Chapter 10, and replace them with a new constitutional framework contained in the schedule to the Bill.

He says this places an enormous responsibility on Parliament.

Seruiratu says governments come and go, Prime Ministers and Opposition Leaders change, political parties rise and fall, and every Member of Parliament will eventually leave public office, but a constitution is intended to endure beyond the political circumstances of the day.

He says Parliament must therefore consider whether the proposed constitutional system will serve Fiji fairly and democratically for generations to come.

The Opposition Leader also says constitutional legitimacy cannot simply be measured by whether consultations were held or submissions received.

He says there is an important distinction between consultation and genuine public ownership, and the key question is whether the final document sufficiently reflects the aspirations, concerns and expectations of the wider population.

Seruiratu says constitutional recognition must also go beyond words in a preamble, with institutions established under the Constitution giving every community confidence that they have a place, a voice and an equal stake in Fiji's future.

He says constitutional reform should never become a contest where recognition of one community is perceived as coming at the expense of another.

Seruiratu also stressed the importance of retaining a common national identity.

He says the strength of a constitution cannot be measured only by the promises contained in its text, but also by whether the institutions it establishes are capable of upholding those promises when they come under pressure.

Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga says amending the 2013 Constitution would bring Fiji's constitutional framework more closely in line with international human rights standards and reflect the belief that human dignity, equality and justice are rights that must be respected and protected.

He says the Bill proposes to remove the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption of Fiji.

The Acting AG says the Bill restores the arrangement by returning investigations to the police and the prosecution to the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Turaga says the retirement age should apply equally to all judges, regardless of their citizenship status.

He says the Bill removes the disparity whereby local judges must retire at 70 years.

Opposition MP Ketan Lal says the Constitution is not an ordinary piece of legislation and therefore any changes to it must be guided by fundamental principles.

Lal says questions must be asked about whether the proposed changes protect citizens and hold the government accountable.

The Opposition MP says constitutional reform should pass the democratic test and any change must be justified.

item.title: Police launch investigation into video showing young boy being assaulted
item.description: Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu says the Internal Affairs Department has been directed to quickly identify the person seen in the video. Tudravu says if the individual is confirmed to be a police officer, authorities will ensure the safety of the child and take the necessary action.
item.content:encoded:
Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu says the Internal Affairs Department has been directed to quickly identify the person seen in the video.

Tudravu says if the individual is confirmed to be a police officer, authorities will ensure the safety of the child and take the necessary action.

He says such behaviour will not be tolerated and disciplinary and criminal investigations will be pursued where appropriate.

item.title: 10 patient monitors boost Emergency Department, replacing units installed around 2013
item.description: 10 new patient monitors have been handed over to the Emergency Department at the CWM Hospital by the International Women’s Association and GE Healthcare to strengthen patient monitoring and support doctors and nurses during emergencies. IWA President Judy Compain says she recently witnessed two patients being resuscitated at the hospital and saw monitors being moved between them.
item.content:encoded:
10 new patient monitors have been handed over to the Emergency Department at the CWM Hospital by the International Women’s Association and GE Healthcare to strengthen patient monitoring and support doctors and nurses during emergencies.

IWA President Judy Compain says she recently witnessed two patients being resuscitated at the hospital and saw monitors being moved between them.

Compain says she later contacted a doctor at the hospital to find out how many monitors were available in the Emergency Department and was told there were only three.

She says the Emergency Department is often where people first come into contact with the health system, particularly when they are facing some of the most difficult moments of their lives.

Compain says after asking how many monitors were needed, the department eventually settled on 10.

She says every minute matters in an emergency, and doctors and nurses need to be able to see at a glance what is happening with a patient.

Compain says patient monitors provide clinicians with continuous and reliable information, allowing them to identify when a patient's condition is deteriorating, act quickly and focus their attention where it is needed most.

She says in a busy Emergency Department, the monitors can work like an extra pair of eyes for doctors and nurses.

She acknowledges the long hours and pressure faced by health workers, and says the community should ensure they have the equipment they need to carry out their work.

Compain says the donation was made possible through the generosity and hard work of IWA members, sponsors, supporters and friends.

She also thanked the Ministry of Health, FPBS and Biomed for their assistance with the equipment.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Deepak Sharma says the Emergency Department's previous monitors were installed around 2013 to 2014 and had gone well beyond their intended period of use.

Dr Sharma says the old monitors helped the department through the COVID-19 pandemic, but it was time to replace them.

He says there had been several roadblocks and challenges in securing new monitors, but the department is now receiving new monitors for patients in the resuscitation area, as well as mobile monitors.

Dr Sharma says the mobile monitors will allow staff to continue monitoring patients wherever they are in the Emergency Department, particularly when the department is access-blocked.

He says the new equipment is a major boost for the Emergency Department and thanked IWA and GE Healthcare for helping make the handover possible.

Dr Sharma also conveyed the appreciation of the Acting Medical Superintendent, who was unable to attend the handover because of another meeting.

He says the doctors, nurses and the entire Emergency Department team are sincerely grateful for the support.

item.title: More than 10,000 attend USP Open Day, students explore future careers
item.description: More than 10,000 students, teachers and families attended the Westpac USP 2026 Open Day, with Year 13 students exploring study options, career pathways and opportunities available at the University of the South Pacific. Students travelled from across Fiji, including from remote and maritime islands, to attend the Open Day at the Laucala, Lautoka and Labasa campuses.
item.content:encoded:
More than 10,000 students, teachers and families attended the Westpac USP 2026 Open Day, with Year 13 students exploring study options, career pathways and opportunities available at the University of the South Pacific.

Students travelled from across Fiji, including from remote and maritime islands, to attend the Open Day at the Laucala, Lautoka and Labasa campuses.

The annual event gives prospective students an opportunity to learn more about USP’s academic programmes, admission pathways, student support services and the different opportunities available during their university journey.

This year’s Open Day was held with the theme “Where Culture Meets Excellence”, highlighting the connection between Pacific heritage and world-class higher education.

Year 13 student Leilani Wong from St Joseph’s Secondary School says she learned more about climate change, including the issue of saltwater intrusion and changes to Fiji’s environment over the past decade.

Wong says she wants to learn more about USP and explore areas outside her comfort zone.

She says she is planning to attend USP and is particularly interested in the Geographic Information Systems course.

Her schoolmate Veniana Wara says she learned about sustainability, marine life and global warming during the Open Day.

Wara says she is interested in Computer Science and hopes to explore the programme during her visit.

She says she is looking forward to attending USP next year because of the facilities and opportunities available.

Year 13 student Mesake Cakau from Marist Brothers High School in Kadavu says the Open Day has helped him learn more about his future career.

Cakau is considering a Bachelor of Agriculture and says he learned about the requirements for the programme and the career opportunities available.

He says he has not yet made a final decision on which university he will attend, but believes education is important, especially when students face challenges in their chosen fields.

Year 13 Queen Victoria School students Charles Koroi and Archie William also attended the Open Day.

Koroi says USP has given them an opportunity to think about their long-term goals and explore different career paths.

Insert: Koroi and William on career paths 2nd Oct 26

Koroi plans to pursue Law and encourages young people to look ahead, set long-term goals and study hard.

William says USP offers a wide range of career paths and he was impressed by the university’s equipment and friendly staff.

He plans to pursue Civil Engineering and also encourages young people to work hard and make use of the educational opportunities available.

USP Pro-Chancellor and Chair of Council and the Interim Management Group, Right Honourable Siosiua Utoikamanu, says choosing a university is about preparing for the world students will enter and the contribution they hope to make to their families, communities and the region.

Utoikamanu says USP belongs to the Pacific and has served the region for nearly six decades.

He says students are entering a rapidly changing world, with technology and artificial intelligence transforming how people learn and work.

Utoikamanu says students can embrace new technology while remaining grounded in their identity and communities.

The Cook Islands Campus will conclude USP’s Open Day series next month for prospective students.
